lead: An air-standard cycle is a clean estimate, but a real engine runs on a fuel-air mixture whose specific heats change with temperature. A fuel-air cycle keeps the ideal cycle shape and adds a real mixture, variable specific heats, dissociation and finite combustion. It still has no friction and no pumping loss. Actual cycle analysis then adds gas exchange, heat loss, blowdown, exhaust, friction and incomplete combustion, and reads these from an indicator diagram. Engineers use the three levels to see where the gap between textbook efficiency and measured efficiency comes from.
prereq: You need: ideal air-standard cycles from Chapter 1.7, valve timing from Chapter 1.5, and SI/CI working from Chapter 1.4.

sections.h3: Fuel-air cycle: real mixture, still ideal

blocks.text: An air-standard cycle uses air alone as the working fluid, constant specific heats, and heat added from outside. A fuel-air cycle keeps the same cycle outline (compression, heat release, expansion, heat rejection) but uses a mixture of fuel vapour and air. It also lets specific heat rise with temperature, and the heat release is not instantaneous, so the peak pressure is lower and the cycle is closer to a limited-pressure cycle.

The specific heat at constant volume, c_v (J/kg·K), is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of gas by 1 K at constant volume. In real gases c_v increases with temperature. Hot burned gas therefore needs more heat for the same temperature rise, so peak temperature and pressure are lower than the air-standard estimate. Dissociation at high temperature also absorbs energy when CO₂ and H₂O break into CO, H₂, O and OH; part of that energy returns later, but the peak is flattened.

Combustion is finite. The flame needs time to cross the chamber, so pressure rise is not instantaneous. Because heat release is spread over part of the expansion, the fuel-air cycle sits closer to a limited-pressure cycle than to a pure constant-volume Otto cycle. The fuel-air cycle still assumes ideal processes: no friction, no pumping loss, no heat loss to walls, no leakage. It is an ideal cycle with a real mixture.

blocks.where: η_fuel-air is fuel-air cycle efficiency (dimensionless); W_net is net ideal work per cycle (J); Q_in is heat released by the fuel per cycle (J).

blocks.text: At the same compression ratio, fuel-air efficiency is lower than air-standard efficiency. The gap comes from the real mixture, variable c_v and dissociation.

sections.h3: Actual cycle: gas exchange and losses

blocks.text: The actual cycle is the real p–V or p–θ diagram from a running engine. Valve timing from Chapter 1.5 means intake opens before TDC and exhaust closes after TDC. The piston therefore pumps fresh charge and exhaust gas through finite pressure differences. In a naturally aspirated engine the intake line sits below atmospheric pressure and the exhaust line above it. The loop between them is the pumping loop; its area is pumping work, and it reduces net work.

Heat loss to cylinder walls, piston and head removes energy during compression and combustion. The exhaust valve opens before BDC. High-pressure gas blows down through the valve, so the exhaust stroke starts at lower pressure. This avoids pumping high-pressure gas and protects the valve, but some expansion work is lost. Friction in piston rings, bearings, valve train and auxiliaries converts indicated work into heat. Incomplete combustion leaves some fuel energy unburned.

blocks.where: η_i is indicated efficiency; W_i is indicated work per cycle from the indicator diagram (J); Q_fuel is chemical energy supplied by fuel per cycle (J).
η_b is brake efficiency; W_b is brake work per cycle at the shaft (J); η_m = W_b / W_i is mechanical efficiency (dimensionless).

blocks.text: The indicator diagram area gives W_i. The brake work W_b is smaller by friction. For a naturally aspirated engine the pumping loop usually reduces W_i, so its sign matters.

The three cycles form a ladder. Air-standard is the top estimate; fuel-air removes mixture and property errors; actual removes gas-exchange, heat-transfer and friction errors. At the same compression ratio the efficiencies fall in that order.

blocks.text: Falls are compared in percentage points, not percent. A fall from 56.5% to 48.0% is 8.5 percentage points. It is not an 8.5% fall; the relative fall is 8.5/56.5 = 15.0%. Use 'percentage points' in exams.

The actual indicated value does not include friction; brake efficiency would be lower by η_m. Only a few universities teach the full loss breakdown. If your syllabus stops at fuel-air, learn the definitions, the direction of each loss, and the indicator diagram. Detailed loss accounting belongs to Unit 5, Engine Testing and Performance. Emission formation belongs to Unit 6.

figure.caption: Nested sets: the air-standard cycle sits inside the fuel-air cycle, which sits inside the actual cycle. Each outer ring adds effects that lower efficiency; friction and pumping belong only to the actual cycle.

spec.aria: Nested sets place the air-standard cycle inside the fuel-air cycle inside the actual cycle, adding real-mixture and loss effects.

examples.question: An air-standard Otto cycle has efficiency 56.5%. A fuel-air cycle at the same compression ratio has efficiency 48.0%. The actual indicated efficiency is 38.0%. Find the fall from air-standard to fuel-air, from fuel-air to actual, and the overall fall.
steps: Write the three efficiencies: η_air = 56.5%, η_fuel-air = 48.0%, η_actual,i = 38.0%.
Fall from air-standard to fuel-air: η_air − η_fuel-air = 56.5 − 48.0 = 8.5 percentage points.
Fall from fuel-air to actual: η_fuel-air − η_actual,i = 48.0 − 38.0 = 10.0 percentage points.
Overall fall: η_air − η_actual,i = 56.5 − 38.0 = 18.5 percentage points.
examples.answer: The falls are 8.5 percentage points, 10.0 percentage points and 18.5 percentage points overall.
examples.check:
eta_air = 56.5
eta_fuel_air = 48.0
eta_actual = 38.0
fall1 = eta_air - eta_fuel_air
fall2 = eta_fuel_air - eta_actual
overall = eta_air - eta_actual
print(f"{fall1:.1f}")
print(f"{fall2:.1f}")
print(f"{overall:.1f}")

traps: A fuel-air cycle is still ideal. Friction, pumping and wall heat loss belong to the actual cycle; do not subtract them in the fuel-air step.
Percentage points are not percent. A fall from 56.5% to 48.0% is 8.5 percentage points, not an 8.5% fall.
Indicated efficiency is before friction. Brake efficiency is η_i × η_m, so it is lower; do not call η_i the brake efficiency.
Valve timing means the actual cycle is not closed at TDC and BDC. Intake opens before TDC and exhaust closes after TDC; the pumping loop is part of the indicator diagram.
Blowdown before BDC loses expansion work but reduces pumping work. It is not free; state both effects.

quiz.q: List three effects included in a fuel-air cycle but not in an air-standard cycle.
quiz.a: Real fuel-air mixture, variable specific heats, and dissociation or finite combustion.

quiz.q: Why is fuel-air efficiency lower than air-standard efficiency at the same compression ratio?
quiz.a: Variable c_v and dissociation lower peak temperature and pressure. The real mixture changes gas properties, so less peak pressure for the same heat release gives less work.

quiz.q: An air-standard Otto cycle has η = 60.0%, a fuel-air cycle has η = 52.0%, and actual indicated η = 41.0%. Find both falls and the overall fall in percentage points.
quiz.a: 60.0 − 52.0 = 8.0 percentage points; 52.0 − 41.0 = 11.0 percentage points; overall 60.0 − 41.0 = 19.0 percentage points.

quiz.q: A student says: 'The fuel-air cycle includes friction, so I subtract friction before comparing with the actual cycle.' Correct the statement.
quiz.a: The fuel-air cycle is ideal and has no friction. Friction is a mechanical loss between indicated and brake work in the actual engine; subtract it only when moving from indicated to brake.

quiz.q: What is the pumping loop on an indicator diagram?
quiz.a: The loop formed by intake and exhaust stroke pressure differences. Its area is pumping work; in a naturally aspirated engine it reduces net work.

quiz.q: Why does the exhaust valve open before BDC?
quiz.a: To blow down high-pressure gas before the exhaust stroke, reduce pumping work and protect the valve. Some expansion work is lost.

quiz.q: An engine has indicated efficiency 36.0% and mechanical efficiency 85.0%. Find brake efficiency and state which losses are inside η_i and which are added by η_m.
quiz.a: η_b = 0.36 × 0.85 = 0.306 = 30.6%. η_i contains pumping, heat loss, blowdown and incomplete combustion; η_m adds friction and auxiliary losses.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engine developers use 1-D gas-exchange simulation and measured cylinder pressure to calibrate fuel-air and actual-cycle models. Search for 'fuel-air cycle simulation', 'variable specific heat combustion' and 'engine indicator diagram analysis'. Detailed chemistry models add dissociation and knock, while test cells supply the pressure trace. The same ladder appears in turbocharged and hybrid engine calibration.
